edges.effect_quant: In 152,622 Tennessee children, each additional infant antibiotic prescription was associated with 20% higher odds of childhood asthma (aOR 1.20, 95% CI 1.19-1.20); in a Swedish nationwide cohort of 493,785 children, prenatal exposure showed HR 1.28 in the cohort analysis but 0.99 in sibling analysis, while respiratory-indication antibiotics in childhood were linked to HR 4.12 in the cohort and 2.36 in sibling analysis.
edges.population: children exposed to antibiotics during fetal life or infancy in large observational cohorts and birth cohorts
edges.mechanism: Antibiotics may alter early microbial colonization and immune training in ways that could promote later airway inflammation, but the same association can also be inflated by respiratory infections or family-level susceptibility that drive both antibiotic prescribing and asthma risk.
edges.summary: Early-life antibiotic exposure is repeatedly associated with a higher later risk of childhood asthma, especially in large administrative and cohort datasets. The relationship survives some adjustments and dose-response analyses, but it weakens meaningfully once sibling comparisons and confounding-by-indication are considered.
edges.caveats: This is one of the clearest examples where a real observational signal does not automatically mean a clean causal effect. Respiratory infections, clinician prescribing behavior, and shared family factors explain part of the association, so the safest interpretation is harmful association with substantial residual confounding.
